summary: Published as a historical record of version 3.0 of the Secure Sockets Layer protocol, which provides privacy and integrity for client-server communication and was the basis for TLS. It is historic, and SSL 3.0 should not be used today.

plainLanguage.summary: SSL was an early way to put a secret lock on internet conversations. This is a museum copy of the rules. The lock is old and no longer safe.

subtitle: The foundational security protocol that became Transport Layer Security (TLS).

tldr.problem: Internet applications needed a way to communicate securely without eavesdropping, tampering, or forgery, but no standard protocol existed for this before SSL.
tldr.mechanism: SSL 3.0 layers two protocols on top of TCP: a handshake protocol that authenticates parties and negotiates encryption keys, and a record layer that encrypts and authenticates data using those keys.
tldr.outcome: SSL 3.0 became the basis for TLS 1.0 and remains the security foundation of HTTPS and many other internet protocols. It is now historic and cryptographically deprecated, but this RFC serves as the historical reference for the protocol.

today: RFC 6101 is Historic. SSL 3.0 is cryptographically deprecated and should not be used for new applications. It was superseded by TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, TLS 1.2, and most recently TLS 1.3. Modern browsers and servers no longer support SSL 3.0 due to known vulnerabilities, particularly the POODLE attack in 2014.

sections.title: Introduction and Goals
sections.content:
SSL 3.0 is a security protocol designed to provide privacy and reliability between communicating applications over the Internet. The protocol enables client and server applications to communicate in a way designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering, and message forgery.

The primary goals of SSL 3.0, in order of priority, are cryptographic security (establish a secure connection), interoperability (independent implementations should work together), extensibility (accommodate new cryptographic algorithms without redesigning the protocol), and relative efficiency (reduce CPU overhead through session caching and careful protocol design).

SSL 3.0 is application-protocol independent; any protocol can layer on top of it transparently. The protocol provides connection security with three key properties: the connection is private (using encryption), the peer's identity can be authenticated (using public-key cryptography), and the connection is reliable (using message integrity checks).
sections.plainLanguage: SSL is a way for computers to verify who they are talking to and then encrypt their conversation so nobody can eavesdrop. It works with any kind of application.

sections.title: Protocol Layers
sections.content:
SSL is a layered protocol composed of two main layers. The SSL record layer sits directly on top of a reliable transport protocol (like TCP) and handles fragmentation, compression, and encryption of data. The SSL handshake protocol runs on top of the record layer and handles the critical task of establishing a secure connection.

The record layer receives uninterpreted data from higher-level protocols and fragments it into records of 2^14 bytes (16,384 bytes) or less. Records can contain four types of data: change_cipher_spec messages (which signal a transition to new encryption keys), alert messages (errors or warnings), handshake messages (the negotiation protocol), and application_data (the actual encrypted content).

Before transmission, records are optionally compressed, then a Message Authentication Code (MAC) is computed and appended for integrity protection. Finally, the data is encrypted using the negotiated cipher suite. The receiver reverses these steps: decrypt, verify the MAC, decompress, and deliver the data.
sections.plainLanguage: Data goes through several steps: it gets broken into chunks, squished smaller if possible, gets a tamper-check code attached, and then gets scrambled with a code. The other computer does the reverse to read it.

sections.title: The Handshake Protocol
sections.content:
The handshake protocol is how a client and server establish a secure connection. When an SSL client and server first communicate, they go through a structured exchange of messages to agree on a protocol version, select cryptographic algorithms, optionally authenticate each other, and generate shared secrets using public-key encryption.

The handshake typically proceeds as follows: the client sends a ClientHello message listing its supported protocol versions, cipher suites, and compression methods. The server responds with a ServerHello, selecting the options both sides will use. The server then sends its certificate (if it needs to authenticate itself), optionally a ServerKeyExchange message (with key material for certain algorithms), and a ServerHelloDone message.

The client then sends its ClientKeyExchange message (containing its part of the shared secret), optionally a CertificateVerify message (if it sent a certificate), and a ChangeCipherSpec message that signals a switch to the negotiated encryption parameters. It sends a Finished message under the new encryption to prove both sides can correctly compute the keys. The server does the same: it sends its ChangeCipherSpec and Finished message. Once both Finished messages are verified, the handshake is complete and application data can flow.
sections.plainLanguage: The client says 'Hi, here is what I support', the server picks what they will both use and proves who it is, the client proves who it is, and they both confirm they are using the same secret code before talking for real.

sections.title: Cryptographic Operations
sections.content:
SSL 3.0 uses both asymmetric (public-key) cryptography for authentication and key exchange, and symmetric cryptography for bulk data encryption. Common public-key algorithms include RSA (for both key exchange and signing) and Diffie-Hellman (for key exchange only). These operations are used during the handshake to prove identity and establish a shared secret.

The shared secret established during the handshake is used to derive the actual encryption keys and MAC secrets through a process specified in the protocol. The RFC defines a master secret of 48 bytes, shared between client and server, from which smaller keys for encryption and authentication are derived.

For encrypting application data, SSL 3.0 uses symmetric ciphers such as DES, 3DES, or RC4. Message integrity is provided by keyed Message Authentication Codes computed using secure hash functions like SHA-1 or MD5. The MAC is computed before encryption; thus both confidentiality and integrity are protected.

The protocol supports both stream ciphers (like RC4, which generate a pseudorandom keystream) and block ciphers (like DES, which encrypt fixed-size blocks using CBC mode with an initialization vector to ensure identical plaintext blocks produce different ciphertext).
sections.plainLanguage: Special math tricks let computers prove who they are and agree on a secret number. That secret number becomes a key that encrypts all the data. They also attach a fingerprint to each message so the other side can tell if anyone tampered with it.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
The handshake protocol authenticates the server using its certificate and can authenticate the client using a client certificate. Sequence numbers on each message prevent missing, reordered, or replayed messages. The protocol detects downgrade attacks and includes mechanisms to resume previously established sessions for efficiency without sacrificing security.

However, SSL 3.0 has known cryptographic weaknesses. The protocol used MD5 for signature generation, which is now cryptographically broken. The MAC-then-encrypt construction and other design choices have been superseded by better approaches in TLS. For these reasons, SSL 3.0 is deprecated and should not be used for new applications.

RFC 6101 was published in 2011 as a historic reference document. Although SSL 3.0 was never formally published by the IETF before this—it only existed in expired Internet-Drafts—it became the de facto standard and the basis for TLS 1.0, which added improvements and became an official Internet Standard. Modern browsers and servers no longer support SSL 3.0, having moved to TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol proved good at its job—HTTPS and internet banking used it for years. But mathematicians later found weaknesses in the code. Newer versions fixed the problems, so nobody uses the original SSL 3.0 anymore, but we keep this document so people can understand how it worked.
